body:
Animation has many properties, but what is the justification for why this PR only adds guards to three of those properties?

I certainly understand that some resource classes have properties with similar guards. The question here is whether we should confirm the policy on whether properties that call `emit_changed()` should consistently have this guard across all resource classes.

So I don't think there is any reason not to merge this, but similarly, I don't think there is any urgent reason to merge it right now either. Rather than adding such guards one by one, we should probably check the policy and then add them more broadly and consistently.

Anyway, it should be possible to add the same guard on the GDScript side, without any fix for the core.

To clarify the scope: length, loop_mode, and step are actually the only writable properties on the Animation class itself. The track-level functions (like enabling/disabling tracks, changing paths, or interpolation types) belong to a separate category since they operate on individual tracks rather than the animation object as a whole. Happy to extend the same check to track methods if that’s the preferred direction, or leave it for a broader policy decision.

You're right that this can be guarded in script space. However, setting animation properties during state transitions is a pretty common pattern, and it’s non-obvious to users that re-assigning the same value invalidates the cache for all instances sharing that animation. In a quick stress test with 200 identical players, preventing the redundant reset dropped cache clear operations from 120k to 0 and halved the frame time (1.35 ms -> 0.68 ms).

> However, setting animation properties during state transitions is a pretty common pattern

I am skeptical about this. At least the word "pretty common" has got to be wrong.

Basically, you almost never change those properties dynamically. For purposes like changing them, you should probably use interval playback with Markers, or BreakLoopAtEnd in an AnimationTree's StateMachine.

As a case where you absolutely must change them, there might be situations where you procedurally create an Animation as a Resource, but this is not a common use case.

You're right, "pretty common" was an overstatement. 

In my game every creature calls set_loop_mode() before each play(), and all creatures of one kind share the same Animation resource. So whenever one creature changed state, the caches of every mixer using that animation were thrown away and rebuilt. In a headless run with every animation playing, cache rebuilds took 1.7% of the main thread before the change and 0 after it, and the animation cost went down by about 25%. On the phone I measured the difference to be within noise, so it only really shows up when many mixers are active at once.

You're right that a game can guard this in script, and I did that on my side first. What I ran into is that nothing hints that setting the same value invalidates every instance that shares the resource, so it is easy to hit without noticing.

About the policy question: I'm fine with either way. If the rule you want is that emit_changed() is skipped when the value is unchanged, I'm happy to look at doing it consistently across the classes where it applies, rather than only these three setters. Or if you'd rather settle the policy first, I can leave the PR as it is until then. Which do you prefer?
